title: Dizzy Gillespie as teacher; the pianist as 88-string drum
summary: Dizzy has players sing passages and shows Malachi at the piano how comping should be rhythmic and percussive.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: I was talking about Dizzy Gillespie. As I said before, he just has a strong... The things that he taught me were the real turning point in harmony and the way to play, rhythmically and every other way... Dizzy is a great teacher, and he has a very unique way of telling you something or telling you how to do it, that after he tells you, there's just no way that you can't understand what he's talking about. And during the whole time that he rehearsed the band, whenever someone was having a problem with a passage, he always... I never heard him use the expression "Play this" or "Play that." He would have a guy play the passage, and then he would tell him, "No, that's not it." He said, "Don't play it. Say it. Say so-and-so," and then he would hum the passage. And after that, whoever he was showing this particular thing to would get it right away. It was just small things like that.

But with me, Dizzy would come to the piano, and he would sit down and actually show me on the piano just what he was doing, or just what to do. He was always encouraging me, because he liked me as a pianist and an arranger. Which he used to make comments about me that made me feel very good, because I had all this respect for him. Even in playing accompaniment on the piano, there were times that he would

come back after the number was over and tell me something that I did in playing with the band, or in accompanying the soloist or something that I shouldn't have done. For example, if we were playing a fast number or something like that, and a chord was, say, two measures or one measure or something like that, and I would sustain it as a whole note or something, and it's an up-tempo tune, he would come back and say, 'No, don't do it like that.' He would show me a rhythmic way to do it which showed me that the pianist was in the rhythm section, is a percussionist.... The percussionist aspects of the instrument is displayed more than some of the more sustained and melodic ways of playing it. Because he said that when you play it like that, it helps the rhythm to move. What you've got is an 88-stringed drum when you're playing the piano in the rhythm section, you know. And you do certain things that complement the soloists and that parallels what the drummer is doing, as well as the rhythmic instruments in the rhythm section -- the bass and...at that particular time we had a guitar, too.
